title: Roopkund (Skeleton Lake)
sources: Harney et al., 'Ancient DNA from the skeletons of Roopkund Lake reveals Mediterranean migrants in India', Nature Communications 10, 3670 (2019)

verified.text: Roopkund is a high-altitude glacial lake in the Chamoli district of Uttarakhand, India, in the Himalayas near the Trishul massif.
The lake lies at an altitude of about 5,020 metres (about 16,470 feet).
It is called Skeleton Lake because the remains of several hundred people, estimated at between 300 and 800, lie in and around it.
The remains became widely known in 1942, when a forest ranger, H. K. Madhwal, came across them.
The lake is frozen for most of the year; the bones become visible when the snow and ice melt.
A 2019 study in the journal Nature Communications analysed ancient DNA from 38 of the skeletons.
The study found that the people belonged to genetically distinct groups who died in separate events about 1,000 years apart, not all at once.
One group had South Asian ancestry and died around 800 CE (between the 7th and 10th centuries).
Another group had Eastern Mediterranean ancestry, similar to people from present-day Greece and Crete, and died around 1800 CE.
Roopkund lies on the route of the Nanda Devi Raj Jat pilgrimage, which is held about once every 12 years.

theories.text: Many of the people may have been killed by a sudden, severe hailstorm: a 2004 analysis reported head injuries consistent with blows from large hailstones.
Why the Eastern Mediterranean group was in the Himalayas around 1800 CE is unknown.

legends.text: Local folklore says the goddess Nanda Devi sent a deadly hailstorm to punish King Jasdhaval of Kannauj and his royal pilgrimage party for disrespecting her shrine.

knownErrors.text: Roopkund is in Panna National Park
knownErrors.correction: Roopkund is in the Chamoli district of Uttarakhand (Panna National Park is in Madhya Pradesh).

knownErrors.text: A plane crash killed the people
knownErrors.correction: There is no plane crash; the remains are centuries old.

knownErrors.text: They were Japanese soldiers from World War II
knownErrors.correction: An early wartime guess, disproved by dating: the remains are centuries old.
A forest ranger (H. K. Madhwal) reported them in 1942.

knownErrors.text: All the people died in a single event
knownErrors.correction: DNA and dating show separate events about 1,000 years apart.

uncertain: Nobody knows for certain what killed every group, or why the Mediterranean group was there. Exact numbers of people are estimates.
